rob_tool_version: ROBINS-I, 2016 version (Sterne et al., BMJ 2016;355:i4919), 7 domains plus overall
signalling_responses: Is there potential for confounding of the effect of intervention in this study? Did the authors use an appropriate analysis method that controlled for all the important confounding domains?
rationale: Estimand: the effect of being prescribed antipsychotic medication, versus not being prescribed it, on working at the 20-year follow-up, in a naturalistic non-randomised comparison. The two counts (9 of 36 and 16 of 22) exist in the report only as the two sides of that comparison, which is why ROBINS-I rather than the JBI prevalence checklist is applied: neither count is a whole-cohort prevalence, and neither arm was randomised. This row is the 'prescribed antipsychotics at 20 years' side. Medication status was determined by clinicians and patients, not by the investigators, so confounding by indication is intrinsic: patients who remain on antipsychotics for twenty years differ systematically in illness severity, insight and treatment engagement from those who stop, and the report itself shows that those continuously prescribed antipsychotics were significantly more likely to have negative symptoms, which it also shows predicts not working. The authors address this seriously, with separate analyses controlling for prognostic potential (Vaillant), premorbid developmental achievement (Zigler), psychosis and negative symptoms, and a GEE logistic and proportional-odds model adjusting for prognosis, premorbid functioning and symptoms. Those adjustments are post-hoc, use dichotomised covariates, and cannot address baseline severity determining both medication continuation and work capacity. The specific 20-year comparison reported as 9/36 v. 16/22 is unadjusted.

rationale: Estimand: the effect of being prescribed antipsychotic medication, versus not being prescribed it, on working at the 20-year follow-up, in a naturalistic non-randomised comparison. rob_tool_version: JBI critical appraisal checklist for studies reporting prevalence data (Munn et al., 2020)
rationale: Two distinct problems. First, the rating is retrospective file extraction: 'Data were gathered retrospectively, and are based on case notes written by numerous clinicians whose inter-rater reliability could not be evaluated', and reliability was established only between the two auditors for CGI-S, GAF and insight, not for the vocational index. Second, the point at which the condition was measured differs between participants: outcome was taken 'at the time of discharge (either at the end of 18 months of treatment or on the basis of the last file-entry if patients moved out of catchment area, disengaged or had died)', with time in service ranging from under 1 week to 208 weeks. A prevalence measured at systematically different elapsed times is not measured in a standard way across the cohort.

rationale: Twenty consenting EIP teams were allocated 1:1 online through Sealed Envelope with a randomly generated sequence produced by the Brighton and Sussex Clinical Trials Unit, permuted blocks of length 2, stratified by site, so the sequence generation and concealment are adequate at cluster level. Participants were identified after their team was allocated, from consecutive referrals, which leaves scope for identification bias, and the arms came out markedly unequal in size (652 versus 375 from 11 versus 9 teams). rob_tool_version: Cochrane RoB 2 (Sterne et al., 2019), effect of assignment to intervention
rationale: Analysis followed intention-to-treat principles and the comparison is of assignment rather than adherence, which is appropriate. Delivery, however, fell well short of plan: expected fidelity was a score of 3 or above but median scores were 2 to 2.3 out of 4, only 7 of 11 teams reached 3 or more, fidelity fell from early to late intervention in 83% of teams, and 12 to 16 months of the intervention period ran during COVID-19, which stopped social engagement entirely and restricted the goal-focused alliance. Both arms also delivered NICE-recommended vocational interventions as part of standard care, so the contrast on a socio-occupational outcome is narrower than the labels suggest.

rob_tool_version: Cochrane RoB 2 (Sterne et al., 2019), effect of assignment to intervention
rationale: This is the dominant problem for this result. Socio-occupational data were collected only from the 232 of 1027 participants (22.6%) who consented to the societal cost-effectiveness interview: 456 did not consent and 339 were lost to follow-up or not approached. The estimate comes from multiple imputation over that base, and the authors themselves say the findings 'must be viewed cautiously as only 22% consented to provide data'. The consenting subsample was demonstrably unrepresentative, with a higher proportion of White ethnicity (59.7%) and fewer males (59.5%) than the whole sample. For the secondary outcomes analysed in the same way the report states that conclusions 'were not robust to departures from the missing-at-random assumption'.

rationale: This is the dominant problem for this result. rationale: A monocentre parallel-group trial with participants 'randomly assigned' and raters blinded to allocation, registered as DRKS00018107. Three things are missing or wrong. No method of sequence generation or allocation concealment is described anywhere. The trial registration postdates the start of recruitment (recruitment began August 2017; the DRKS identifier is a 2019 registration), so allocation cannot be said to have been concealed on the registry's evidence. And the CONSORT flow does not reconcile: 502 were assessed and 369 found not eligible, which leaves 133, but the box reads 'Eligible for randomization (n = 119)', and 119 minus the 23 not randomised is 96 rather than the 110 shown as randomised. Every step from 110 downwards does reconcile (56 and 54 allocated, 8 lost before T0 in each arm, 2 excluded from each, 46 and 44 analysed), so the outcome denominators are unaffected. Baseline PANSS negative scores differ appreciably (11.4 IPS versus 13.7 TAU).

rob_tool_version: ROBINS-I (Sterne et al., 2016)
rationale: Assignment to LICM was made by the programme on clinical grounds, and the groups differ sharply on almost everything that predicts employment. LICM participants were younger (42.6 versus 50.7 years), far more likely to have active psychotic symptoms (62.5% versus 21.4%), more likely to have a lifetime psychiatric admission (60.9% versus 22.7%) and an admission in the past year (17.5% versus 2.0%), more likely to have used illicit drugs (23.4% versus 6.8%), and much less likely to be employed at baseline (23.4% versus 48.9%). rob_tool_version: JBI critical appraisal checklist for studies reporting prevalence data (Munn et al.), 9 items
rationale: The estimand is employment prevalence in a first-episode psychosis population, and the frame is the complete treated incidence of a defined catchment. EPPIC is a state-funded service covering 'a defined catchment area within northern and western Melbourne' with over a million residents and 166,760 aged 15-24, and the authors state 'there are no other public mental health services in the catchment area which provide treatment to people with a first episode of psychosis who are aged 15 to 24 at the time of presentation'. All psychotic disorders including drug-induced psychosis were included. The residual gap is people treated privately or not treated at all.
source_location: Methods, Setting, p. 1390; Methods, Participants, p. 1390

rob_tool_version: JBI critical appraisal checklist for studies reporting prevalence data (Munn et al.), 9 items
rationale: Total enumeration rather than sampling: 'All eligible clients registered with EPPIC between 1 January 2011 and 31 December 2016 were included', and a consent waiver was granted expressly so that no case would be lost, 'As it was essential to ensure that all cases of first episode of psychosis were included and therefore the cohort would be representative, a waiver of individual consent was granted'. No volunteer or convenience selection operates.
source_location: Methods, Participants, p. 1390; Methods, Ethical approval, p. 1391

rob_tool_version: JBI critical appraisal checklist for studies reporting prevalence data (Munn et al.), 9 items
rationale: 1220 presented over six years and 1196 have complete data, with 293 migrants and 903 Australian-born. That is ample for a prevalence estimate; the imprecision of the employment estimate is negligible relative to the construct and timing problems.
source_location: Results, Baseline characteristics, p. 1391

rob_tool_version: JBI critical appraisal checklist for studies reporting prevalence data (Munn et al.), 9 items
rationale: Table 1 gives age, sex, marital status, living arrangements, housing, baseline employment, family history, DSM-IV diagnostic group and comorbid substance use for the whole cohort and both subgroups, and Table 2 gives country of birth at three levels of the Standard Australian Classification of Countries. The service model, catchment and duration of care are described in detail.
source_location: Table 1, p. 1392; Table 2, p. 1393; Methods, Setting, p. 1390

rob_tool_version: JBI critical appraisal checklist for studies reporting prevalence data (Munn et al.), 9 items
rationale: 24 of 1220 (2.0 per cent) were dropped for missing place of birth, which is trivial. The employment row of Table 3 carries no reduced n and its percentages are computed on the full 293 and 903, and the methods state occupation 'was obtained from the discharge summary or progress notes for each young person'. But the four HoNOS rows of the SAME table print explicitly reduced denominators of 830, 839, 831 and 746, which shows that chart-based ascertainment was NOT complete for every measure and that the authors report reduced denominators when they have them. Whether the employment row is genuinely complete or simply not counted is not established, so n_outcome_observed = 1196 carries residual uncertainty.
source_location: Table 3, p. 1394; Methods, Study design & sources of information, p. 1391; Results, p. 1391

rob_tool_version: JBI critical appraisal checklist for studies reporting prevalence data (Munn et al.), 9 items
rationale: Read as ascertainment of the EMPLOYMENT outcome, consistent with every JBI assessment in this shard. The counted condition is a composite: 'being an engaged student or having regular employment made one eligible for the "working or studying" group'. Paid work is not separable from study, 'regular employment' is never defined (no hours, no pay, no contract type), and the measure therefore does not identify paid employment at all. It is a valid EET-family measure and an invalid paid-work measure.
source_location: Methods, Study design & sources of information, p. 1391

rob_tool_version: JBI critical appraisal checklist for studies reporting prevalence data (Munn et al.), 9 items
rationale: Measurement is retrospective abstraction from discharge summaries and progress notes written for clinical rather than research purposes, by the study authors, with no standardised instrument, no stated coding rules beyond the one sentence defining the group, and no inter-rater reliability. The authors concede the analogous problem for symptoms, that measurement 'was reliant on the quality of the clinical notes and the interpretation of these notes by the authors'.
source_location: Methods, Study design & sources of information, p. 1391; Discussion, Strengths and limitations, p. 1396

rob_tool_version: JBI critical appraisal checklist for studies reporting prevalence data (Munn et al.), 9 items
rationale: The comparative analyses (chi-square, Cox regression with age and sex adjustment, proportional-hazards checking) are appropriate for the paper's own aims. For the prevalence estimand the analysis is a bare proportion with no confidence interval, and the two printed values for the migrant rate, 46.8 per cent in Table 3 against 47.3 per cent in the text, are not reconciled anywhere.
source_location: Methods, Statistical analysis, p. 1391; Table 3, p. 1394; Results, Functioning, p. 1395

rob_tool_version: JBI critical appraisal checklist for studies reporting prevalence data (Munn et al.), 9 items
rationale: No response rate is definable for a chart-based total enumeration with a consent waiver, and non-participation bias is correspondingly low. But the outcome is measured at DISCHARGE, and the report does not say how many young people had no discharge summary, disengaged permanently or were still open to the service at data extraction; a companion study is cited showing 56 per cent disengaged at some point. The number with no recorded occupation at discharge is not reported.
source_location: Methods, Setting, p. 1390; Table 3, p. 1394

rationale: The frame is not the target population. Recruitment was restricted to outpatients of two Sao Paulo university services 'who expressed a desire for employment', aged 18-45, with 'stable psychiatric symptoms for at least 2 months' and 'good treatment adherence in the psychiatrist's opinion'. The authors say so themselves: 'this is a convenience sample of individuals with high education levels and favorable symptomatology who were undergoing treatment at university outpatient clinics, which sets the analysis within a particular context'. The selection is directly on a determinant of employment.
source_location: Materials and methods, Participants, p. 36; Discussion, p. 39

rationale: Convenience sampling with two further filters: psychiatrists chose whom to invite, and 'Those who had participated in at least 6 meetings were included in the study', so attendance at a prevocational group is itself an entry condition. Neither random nor consecutive.

rationale: 53 enrolled and 45 analysed. The authors state 'The sample size made it impossible to analyze predictors of job retention' and attribute their null cognitive findings to it. A proportion on 45 has a 95 per cent interval spanning roughly 28 to 57 per cent.

rob_tool_version: JBI critical appraisal checklist for studies reporting prevalence data (Munn et al.), 9 items
rationale: 45 of the 53 enrolled were followed for job-search outcome, which is 85 per cent, but the report never settles which of 45 and 53 is the denominator of its own headline figure, and a third base of 44 is implied by the job-duration percentages. source_location: Materials and methods, Study design, p. 37; Results, pp. 38-39

rationale: The condition is defined explicitly and with its threshold: 'those who obtained any kind of paid work, either formal or informal, for at least 30 days'. source_location: Materials and methods, Data analysis and Statistical analysis, p. 37

rationale: Ascertainment is by monthly participant self-report: 'all individuals were followed monthly through in-person meetings or telephone calls to report their participation in job interviews, study and work'. source_location: Materials and methods, Study design, p. 37

rationale: 8 of 53 were lost to the 18-month job-search follow-up and the report gives no reasons for them. source_location: Materials and methods, Study design, p. 37

rob_tool_version: JBI critical appraisal checklist for studies reporting prevalence data (Munn et al.), 9 items
rationale: Trial-origin applicability, recorded as D2 requires. The frame is people who consented to a randomised trial of antipsychotic dose reduction, which excluded anyone with 'an admission to a psychiatric hospital or a mental health crisis within the preceding month', anyone 'being mandated to take their medication through the Mental Health Act' and anyone 'considered to pose a serious risk to themselves or others'. Those exclusions remove the most unwell, who are also the least likely to be employed, so the frame is not a catchment or population frame for a prevalence estimand even though it carries no employment-related restriction and passes the D9 gate.

rob_tool_version: Cochrane RoB 2 (Sterne et al. 2019), 5 domains plus overall
rationale: Sequence generation and concealment are strong: participants 'were randomized to one of the two treatment programs via a computer program operated by an off-site data manager, with no study personnel aware of assignments in advance', stratified by vocational program and by primary psychiatric diagnosis. Against that, the arms differ substantially at baseline on the strongest known predictor of the outcome, high-school completion 84.6 per cent in E-VR against 50.0 per cent in TSW (chi-square 7.27, p = 0.007), which the authors judged large enough to enter as a covariate. With 54 participants and roughly fifteen baseline comparisons a chance imbalance of this size is possible, so the process is not judged to have failed; but an imbalance this consequential on this small a trial is more than nothing.

rationale: Open-label by necessity: participants, vocational specialists and cognitive specialists all knew the assignment. rob_tool_version: ROBINS-I V2 (2016)

The authors state that "patient inclusion in Morpheus was not standardised, which made it challenging to identify a comparable population in Aalborg" and that the 60% Aalborg eligibility estimate exceeds the 41% actually treated in Aarhus, so the comparator is defined partly after the fact.

rob_tool_version: JBI checklist for prevalence studies (2020)

rob_tool_version: JBI checklist for prevalence studies (2020)

rob_tool_version: JBI checklist for prevalence studies (2020)
rationale: 46% attrition by 24 months, with the analysis base changing from 199 to 166 to 154 to 107 across Table 2b and no imputation or sensitivity analysis. rationale: Two coverage failures. Second, the denominator behind the year-by-year percentages is never stated and cannot be the full 21,551 given accrual to 2016 against linkage ending 31 December 2016 and a median follow-up of 4.8 years.

rationale: Participants were not blinded ('the participants were not blinded to their condition') and the same three psychiatric nurses delivered both the IPS and the ISE protocols, with the authors recording that 'Potential bias may have existed among employment specialists because of the effect of allegiance ... they may have favored the ISE participants'. Against this, allocation to specialists was balanced across IPS and ISE, fidelity was rated at 85-91 per cent in both, and the analysis is stated to be intention-to-treat.
